title: Scurvy in Paediatrics
subject: Paediatrics
summary: Scurvy is a vitamin C deficiency that impairs collagen synthesis, causing fragile tissues, bleeding gums, bruising and poor wound healing. In low‑resource settings it mimics infections and anaemia, so a high index of suspicion is key.

sections.p: Scurvy is the clinical syndrome of vitamin C deficiency. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by history of low fruit/veg intake and typical signs. Laboratory confirmation is rarely needed in resource‑poor settings.
b: Classic signs: bleeding gums, perifollicular petechiae, bruising, poor wound healing

t.b: Low levels indicate impaired collagen hydroxylation

sections.p: Severity is graded by clinical features: mild (gums, bruising), moderate (painful joints, anemia), severe (fractures, haemorrhage).
In East Africa, the main cause is inadequate intake of fresh fruit and vegetables. Other contributors include chronic infections, malnutrition, and certain herbal remedies.
b: Low socioeconomic status limiting food diversity

sections.p: Children present with bleeding gums, swollen joints, easy bruising, fatigue, and poor wound healing. In severe cases, bone pain and fractures occur.
b: Delayed wound healing and poor dentine formation

sections.p: Investigations are supportive; focus on ruling out mimickers and assessing severity.

t.b: Normal or mild changes in scurvy
Supports diagnosis when combined with clinical picture

sections.p: Urgent complications include haemorrhage, severe anaemia, and fractures. Red flags are sudden severe pain, haemorrhagic shock, or inability to walk.
b: Severe pain out of proportion to injury

sections.p: Treat with vitamin C supplementation and dietary improvement. Supportive care includes iron if anaemic and wound care.
b: Provide analgesia and physiotherapy for joint pain

sections.p: Re‑evaluate after 1–2 weeks; symptoms should improve. Prevention focuses on dietary diversification and community education.
b: Screen high‑risk groups (HIV, TB, malnutrition) for deficiency

sections.p: Scurvy mimics many conditions; key differentials include haemorrhagic anaemia, vitamin A deficiency, and infections.
Normal CRP/ESR may mask infection; serum vitamin C can be falsely normal if recent intake; iron studies may be low in both scurvy and iron deficiency.
b: Iron low in scurvy and iron deficiency; need clinical context

whenToSeekHelp: Severe haemorrhage, sudden severe bone pain, inability to walk, signs of shock

faq.a: Yes, vitamin C is needed for iron absorption; deficiency often leads to normocytic or microcytic anaemia.

faq.q: What foods are good sources of vitamin C in East Africa?
faq.a: Mango, papaya, citrus fruits, leafy greens, beans, and local vegetables like pumpkin and cabbage.
IV is used when oral intake is impossible or in severe cases; otherwise oral supplementation is effective.

exam: A 4‑year‑old presents with swollen gums and bruising; what is the most likely diagnosis? — Scurvy; look for low vitamin C intake and bleeding gums.
What is the first step in management of a child with suspected scurvy? — Start vitamin C supplementation and dietary advice.
Which laboratory test would help differentiate scurvy from iron‑deficiency anaemia? — Serum iron and ferritin; low iron with normal ferritin suggests scurvy.
A child with scurvy develops a fracture; what complication should you monitor? — Haemorrhage and delayed healing; monitor haemoglobin and wound healing.
Why are NSAIDs contraindicated in scurvy? — They increase bleeding risk from fragile capillaries.
In a low‑resource setting, how would you confirm scurvy if serum vitamin C is unavailable? — Rely on clinical signs (bleeding gums, petechiae) and dietary history.
What red flag would prompt urgent referral of a child with suspected scurvy? — Severe haemorrhage or inability to walk.
